newsitem.title: LUXEMBOURG: Little hope for OECD shibuilding deal - van Miert.
newsitem.headline: Little hope for OECD shibuilding deal - van Miert.

text.p: European Union Competition Commissioner Karel Van Miert acknowledged on Thursday that he saw only slight hope of the United States ratifying an international deal to slash shipbuilding subsidies in the world.

Van Miert also recognised that most EU countries would oppose implementing the accord struck in 1994 within the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) without U.S. participation, an EU official said.

The Belgian commissioner, who visited the United States last week, spoke at a meeting of EU industry ministers, who debated the sensitive issue of support to Europe's shipbuilding industry, still in difficulties despite severe restructuring.

Van Miert told ministers there was a only a "faint hope now" that the United States would succeed in securing approval for the OECD accord in the Republican-controlled Congress, the EU official told reporters.
In view of this, van Miert presented different options for future EU ship aid rules in the absence of U.S. ratification and said the Commission could soon come forward with proposals.

The United States is the only country which has not ratified the OECD accord -- supposed to have come into force early last year -- to end direct shipbuilding subsidies except social aid, research and development aid.
Among other things, U.S. shipyards argue they have not had enough time to adjust to the commercial era after the loss of military contracts after the end of the Cold War.

If the United States does not ratify the deal, the EU could either apply normal EU state aid rules to the shipbuilding sector, extend existing aid rules or agree on a new support regime for the sector, van Miert said.

The European Commission favours new and stricter aid rules and van Miert said the European Commission would be able to present proposals before the end of the summer, provided it received guidance from EU member states.
Such a proposal could include a "one time, last time" principle for restructuring aid to shipyards, he said.
Most ministers seemed to favour a new aid regime but they did not give manyt details, the EU official said.
However, they differed strongly on the need to prolong existing rules, which expire by the end of this year and which allow for ship aid of up to nine percent of contract value.
The three Nordic EU members, Britain and the Netherlands either argued against prolonging current rules or stressed that such an extension should be for only a very short time.
In contrast, France said the ship aid directive should be prolonged for two more years in view of the strategic importance of the sector in Europe.
The shipbuilding sector is the only European manufacturing industry which still receives substantial amounts of operating aid as a result of the severe crisis in the 1970s and the 1980s.
The industry has gone through tough restructuring, slashing the workforce and capacity by more than half since 1976.

The ministers are expected later on Thursday to give the green light to restructuring aid to struggling German, Greek and Spanish shipyards despite criticism of Nordic EU states which argue it may send the wrong signal to Washington.

U.S. Trade Representative Charlene Barshefsky has expressed "dismay" at the proposal by the EU executive to approve the requests of Bonn, Madrid and Athens, questioning how the state aid would fit with commitments under the OECD deal.

However, EU Competition Commissioner Karel Van Miert has dismissed the criticism, noting that the EU, unlike the United States, had ratified the OECD deal in time and that the three restructuring cases were agreed before the OECD deal was signed.
